directAnswer: Pope Sylvester III, previously John, bishop of Sabina, was elected in January 1045 after a revolt drove Benedict IX from Rome. He held the city only until March or April 1045, and in 1046 the Council of Sutri deposed him, though the Church still lists him among the popes.

sections.h2: The Bishop of Sabina Is Elected
paras: John was bishop of Sabina, a diocese northeast of Rome. When Roman nobles, probably with the support of the Crescentii family, drove Benedict IX out of the city in 1044, they elected John in January 1045. He took the name Sylvester.

Benedict's family remained powerful outside Rome. By March 1045 Benedict had returned and forced Sylvester out. Sylvester went back to his diocese of Sabina. Because his election occurred while Benedict had not resigned, its validity was questioned then and later.

In December 1046 King Henry III convened a council at Sutri to settle the competing claims to the papacy. The council deposed Sylvester and sentenced him to confinement in a monastery. In practice he seems to have returned to his role as bishop of Sabina, where he appears in records for years afterward, until about 1062. The Vatican's official list includes him, while noting the uncertainty around his status.

keyFacts: Reigned 16 January 1045 to 10 April 1045 (per the official list)
Elected after a Roman revolt expelled Benedict IX
Deposed at the Council of Sutri in 1046

faqs.question: Why is Sylvester III's legitimacy questioned?
faqs.answer: He was elected while Benedict IX had not resigned, so many contemporaries and later historians doubted the validity of his election.

faqs.question: What happened to Sylvester III after his deposition?
faqs.answer: The Council of Sutri ordered him confined to a monastery, but records suggest he continued as bishop of Sabina for years.
